title: Is it permissible to take a second wife in Islam?
headline: Four schools permit up to four wives, conditioned on fair treatment between them

summary.text: The four schools allow a free Muslim man to marry up to four wives at once, with the Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali books each stating the cap of four and tying it to the condition of justice. The verse at Quran 4:3 sets the limit at two, three or four and directs a man who fears he cannot be just to one wife. Recent fatwas from the Permanent Committee and Egypt's Dar al-Ifta permit up to four for a man who trusts himself to be just and forbid more than four.

paragraphs.text: The ruling verse is Quran 4:3, which permits marrying two, three or four women and then says that if a man fears he will not be just, he should marry only one. The verse follows a command to hand orphans their wealth and precedes the command to give women their bridal gifts outright, and the surah opens by invoking taqwa and the wombs. The number is therefore capped and the cap is immediately tied to justice.

Ghaylan ibn Salama embraced Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet commanded him to choose four of them; the narration in Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1128 is graded sahih by Ahmad Muhammad Shakir, al-Albani and Bashar Awad Maarouf, and hasan by Zubair Ali Zai. The Ibn Majah version, "Choose four of them", is sahih by al-Albani and Muhammad Fouad Abd al-Baqi, and hasan by Zubair Ali Zai. Qays ibn al-Harith entered Islam with eight wives and was likewise told to keep four; the narration is hasan sahih by al-Albani and Abd al-Baqi but daif by Shu'ayb al-Arnaut and Zubair Ali Zai in Ibn Majah, and in Abu Dawud it is sahih by al-Albani and Muhammad Muhyi al-Din Abd al-Hamid and daif by Zubair Ali Zai.

A hadith in Sunan an-Nasa'i 3942 warns that whoever has two wives and inclines toward one more than the other will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of his body leaning; al-Albani and Abu Ghuddah grade it sahih and Zubair Ali Zai grades it daif. Al-Uthaymeen explains that the warning falls on blameworthy favouritism, not on feelings, citing Sunan Abi Dawud 2133, which al-Albani graded sahih. The Prophet himself had nine wives at once, established in Sahih al-Bukhari 284 and 5215 and Sunan an-Nasa'i 3196, the last graded sahih and agreed upon.

Ali's proposal to the daughter of Abu Jahl while married to Fatima is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari 5230, Sahih Muslim 2449d, Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3869 (hasan sahih) and Sunan Ibn Majah 1999, all sahih, and the Prophet said Fatima is a part of him and what harms her harms him. Aisha's jealousy of Khadija is similarly authentic.

Al-Marghinani in al-Hidaya states that a free man may marry four, free or slave, and may not marry more than that, citing Quran 4:3. Al-Jassas holds that he may take two, three or four as he wishes and steps down a level if he fears injustice. Ibn Rushd records that the Muslims agreed on the permissibility of four free women at once, and that their disagreement fell on the slave's share and on anything above four.

Al-Shirbini in Mughni al-Muhtaj says "for the free man, four only", and also that it is a Sunnah not to marry more than one wife if there is no apparent need; al-Mawardi in al-Hawi holds four permitted and one advised. Malik in al-Mudawwana states that a man who becomes Muslim with ten wives keeps four of his choosing, whether the marriages were in one contract or several. Ibn Rushd reports Malik's position that a slave may have four, against Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i who said two.

Al-Buhuti in Kashshaf al-Qina' states that the free man may not combine more than four wives, citing the Ghaylan and Nufayl narrations. Ibn Qudamah records consensus on the cap, the only reported exception being al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim's nine, which he rejects, and he says in al-Sharh al-Kabir that it is more appropriate to marry only one wife. Al-Nawawi rules that a man who contracts six women in three separate contracts without knowing the order has a valid single-wife contract on every assumption, because she can only fall within the first four.

Quran 4:3 makes justice a condition, while Quran 4:129 says a man will never be able to be equal in feeling between wives even if he strives to do so, and directs him not to incline completely toward one and leave another hanging. The reconciliation is that the required justice is the outward, measurable kind, in maintenance, clothing, housing and the division of nights, which is within a man's power, while the impossible kind is equality of love and desire, and the blame falls on deliberate, total inclination. Al-Uthaymeen explains the hadith's "leaning" as the inclination for which a person is blamed.

Some contemporary writing reads Quran 4:3 as permitting a second wife only in the orphan context. The fatwa and tafsir sources reject that as a restriction: the orphan clause is the occasion that prompted the verse, the command then addresses women generally, and the Prophet fixed the ceiling at four for everyone.

On whether one wife is better or more than one, the Shafi'i and Hanbali books prefer one where there is no need, the Hanafi al-Jassas treats the choice as open, al-Albani and the Dhahiri school lean the other way, and IslamQA calls plural marriage recommended with conditions. Islamweb resolves it by making the answer depend on the man: one is better for the man content with one, and more for the man who genuinely needs more. IslamOnline and AboutIslam stress that it is an option and an exception rather than the norm, and that a man with one wife is not lesser in the sight of Allah.

On the Prophet's nine wives, al-Uthaymeen holds that more than four was a privilege specific to the Prophet, while the community is held to four by Quran 4:3 and the Ghaylan narration. Quran 33:37, where Allah Himself gave Zaynab to the Prophet, is part of that special standing.

Some cite the Prophet's refusal to let Ali marry Abu Jahl's daughter as proof that a first wife's consent is required. Al-Albani answers that the report states its own cause and is specific to the Prophet's family, and the Permanent Committee and Dar al-Ifta both conclude consent is not a legal condition, though concealment and disregard for the first wife's pain are condemned.

The Permanent Committee in Saudi Arabia held it permissible to marry up to four if a man trusts himself to be just, and forbidden beyond four, on the Book, the Sunnah and consensus. It also held that the first wife's consent is not a condition, while kindness toward her is part of good character. Egypt's Dar al-Ifta said the same about consent, described polygamy as a measure to solve social problems rather than to satisfy whims, and advised obeying countries whose laws require the first wife's consent.

IslamQA describes plural marriage as recommended subject to financial and physical ability and justice, and forbidden as a display of extravagance. Islamweb lists the conditions and notes a second wife may waive maintenance or her share of nights by agreement. IslamOnline sets out that polygamy takes any of the five rulings according to circumstance, from obligatory to forbidden, and that it is disliked or forbidden where a man lacks the means or the intention to be fair.

The Hanafi Darul Iftaa calls it permissible with conditions, unwise without genuine need, and a serious error to condemn someone who practices it. Al-Albani advises the able man to marry two, three or four, with justice as the condition, and rejects the claim that Islam only commands one wife and allows a second out of dire necessity.
